en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Yun’an Zhenjing:
The woodblocks for the Recorded Sayings of Master Zhenjing remain at Yujia; students find them difficult to obtain. Whenever they do obtain them, they subsequently lose them.

This is because patch-robed monks (nàzǐ) cherish it so deeply. The Venerable Guantan of Bāngshān had the woodblocks re-carved and printed [this work], as it was at this site that Shu Wang established a temple and invited the patriarch to open the mountain.
Nevertheless, the "no-brain" single stroke of the man from Guānxī will certainly not be found within this record; those who read it should first possess the eye of discernment.

First Month of the Bingzi Year Written with reverence by the Bhikṣu Shouchong of Zhongshan Preface to the Table of Contents for the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Zhenjing of Yun’an (Bhikṣu Shouchong; Su Che)

Verses, Upper Volume, Fifth Verse; Verses, Middle [Volume] (Note: This appears to be a bibliographic or structural heading for a section of a Buddhist scripture, likely from a Chinese translation of a Sanskrit work such as the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* or a similar treatise. The term "偈頌" (*gāthā*) refers to verses; "上卷第五" indicates the fifth verse of the upper volume; and "中" indicates the middle volume.)

Petition Submitted by the Grand Chancellor:

I humbly submit this memorial. In establishing this temple of benevolence, we seek to perpetuate Your Majesty’s sagely longevity. By turning our sincere hearts toward the Great Guide, we open the way for supreme conditions.
The Elder Master Wén has alone received the orthodox transmission; having successively refuted frivolous disputations, he has sought the direction of the mind and initiated his spiritual progress.
Respectfully revering that which is pursued and honored as the ancestral source, I humbly reflect upon Your Compassion, Your Pity, Your Kindness, and Your Diligent Aspiration.
I have prepared this brief record on the day of the third month in the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era.

Written by Wang Anshi, Grand Master of the Hall of Literary Splendor, Commissioner of the Jixi Observation Post, Acting Minister of Works, Grand Marshal, Duke of Jing, with a fief of nine thousand five hundred households and a private grant of three thousand households.
Stone Memorial. Memorial Submitted by the Vice President of the Left, the Governor-General, in Petition:

I humbly submit that you have bestowed upon this site a grove and garden of verdant fields, where magnificent structures flourish; you have established this ground as a site for the Blue Lotus, gracing it with imperial favor.
To extend blessings for longevity and auspiciousness under such a noble name, and to elucidate the principle of sublime requital, one must rely upon those of penetrating insight.

To awaken deluded minds, the Elder Master Wénɡōng has long since realized the True Vehicle (*tathāgatagarbha*) and has presided over the pure assembly for a long time. As for the phenomena of mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*), they do not depend on external, false names;

rather, through hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*), one may internally contemplate the true nature (*dharmatā*). He proclaims the esoteric meaning and harmonizes these supreme conditions.

Respectfully submitted on the [blank] day of the third month in the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era. By Wei, Grand Master for the Cultivation of Virtue, Grand Officer of the Middle Grade, Acting Governor of Jiangning Prefecture,
concurrently Commissioner for Encouraging Agriculture within the jurisdiction, and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Forces of the Eastern Circuit of Jiangnan, accompanied by the rank of Shanghujun.
*An Account of the Conduct of Master Yun’an Zhenjing*, compiled by his disciple, the monk Dehong of Gao’an, appended to the memorial submitted by Wang Anli,
Duke of Kaiguo, with a fief of one thousand two hundred households and a substantive grant of four hundred households.
The Master’s name was Kewen. He was the direct successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan. Born in the Zheng family of Wenxiang in Shanfu, he was exceptionally gifted from birth;
even as a young child, his bearing was like that of a divine being. When playing with other children, he would invariably engage them in dialogue and debate.
His speech was strange; those who heard it were startled and bewildered, unable to understand it, whereupon he would simply laugh heartily with a wide grin and depart.
For generations his family had been officials of the gentry. Once grown, he delighted in reading books, attaining mastery naturally without following the instructions of a teacher.

He served his stepmother with the utmost filial piety; however, she was foolish and repeatedly humiliated him. His relatives could not bear to witness his suffering and sent him away to travel and study in various regions. On the road...
Next was the state of Zhuzhou. At the Beita Monastery, the Elder Gui Xiu’s reputation for the Way was at that time already highly esteemed; his eloquence was unimpeded.

[Daosheng] listened intently from the side of the assembly, and moved to such an extent by realization that he wept. He wished to cast off his robes and caps to become a disciple under Xiu. Xiu smiled and said:
"You are a young scholar of wondrous years; you ought to sigh with ambition to attain a high rank and bring glory to your parents.

Why then do you wish to withdraw your traces into solitude? Is it perhaps that your deliberations have not yet matured? Xuanzang replied, "To attain the 'Pass' where the mind is empty is more than merely bringing glory to one's parents;

it will further enable me to save all beings. To withdraw my traces into solitude is not what we have in common. Xuanchong marveled at his resolve and took him in as a disciple. Xuanzang served him diligently for five years.
In one day, at the age of twenty-five, he underwent the novice ordination (*śrāmaṇera*) for which he had trained. The following year, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).

He then traveled to the capitals of Chang’an and Luoyang, soaring through the lecture halls. Regarding the two schools of Xianshou and Cien—the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* (Characteristics) and *Dharmatā* (Nature)—he thoroughly penetrated the subtle depths of all the great sūtras and śāstras.
Unfolding his texts and grasping his fly-whisk, his voice was clear and resonant; his eloquence was like gathering clouds, and scholars relied upon him to propagate the teachings.

Sheng resided at Longmen Mountain in Yanju. Once, while walking along the corridors of the monastery, he saw a clay statue of a bhikṣu with its head covered and eyes closed, appearing as if in meditative concentration.
Suddenly, he felt a sense of self-disappearance and said to his fellow students: "What I have been carrying is like a figure painted by Gu Kaizhi;
though it is said to be a masterpiece of perfection, it is ultimately not alive. Thereupon, he burned his commentaries and treatises, wrapped them in his robe, and traveled south.
Whether in easy or difficult circumstances, in peace or hardship, he traveled through many great *dharmapīṭhas* (monasteries) in various regions.

He held himself in high regard, considering it difficult to find a true teacher. Once he arrived at Yunju to visit the elder master Shun; their exchange of words did not accord, so he left without staying overnight.
He then went to De Shan Ying Chanshi, who was presiding over the night assembly. [De Shan] disparaged former masters, saying, "There is no Sixth Patriarch."
Upon hearing Yunmen’s words, he laughed heartily. At dawn, he set out. Hearing of the reputation of Chan Master Yunfeng Yue, he traveled by double stages to reach Xiangxiang.
By then, Yue had already passed away. He sighed and said, "Since that person is no longer here, where could I not go?
Though the mountains and rivers are beautiful, I have no leisure to travel them. Consequently, he stayed at Daming Mountain for the duration of his journey. One night, he heard a monk...
He recited Yunmen’s words: "The Buddha-dharma is like the moon in the water—is it so? Yunmen replied, "In the clear waves, there is no path through.
At that moment, his mind opened up suddenly. At this time, Master Nan was already residing at Jicui; he went straight to Nan’s hermitage.
Nan asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Mount Gui. Nan said, "It happens that I am not here. He asked, "I wonder, where are you headed?"
"Let us go," said Nan. "Tiantai goes on communal work; Nanyue wanders as a cloud. Nan said, "If that is so, you too may go with ease.
Nan asked, "As for the shoes on your feet, where did you get them? He replied, "I obtained them for seven hundred coins at Mount Lu."
Nan said, "When have you ever attained mastery? The Master pointed and said, "When have you ever not been masterful? Nan was greatly startled.
He remained to study under him for a long time before taking his leave. Upon reaching West Mountain, he spoke with the elder Chuan of Cuiyan during the night.
Chuan exclaimed in admiration, "This is the one who will revive Linji! Take good care of yourself. At this, the Master’s mind also became clear and expansive, and he felt deep gratitude.
He was one who appreciated true sound. When Master Nangong resided at Huanglong, [Zhaozhou] went again to visit him.

Master Nangong once said to the Master, "Just now I had an attendant roll up the curtain and asked him, 'When the curtain is rolled up, what is it like? He replied, 'It illuminates the whole world. I asked, 'When the curtain is let down, what is it like?
He replied, 'Not a drop of water can pass through. I asked, 'What is it like when it is neither rolled up nor let down? The attendant was speechless. You—"
"How is it? the Master asked. Nan replied, "Only when you, Master, take the place of the attendant and descend to the Nirvana Hall will it be possible.

Nan spoke these words with a stern glare, saying, "A man from Guansi truly has no sense. He then looked toward a monk standing nearby. The Master pointed at him and said, "Even this monk has not yet seen a dream.
Master Nan simply smiled. Chan Master Longqing Xian was a close friend of the Master; at that time, he was serving as the guest prefect.
Xian asked, "Head Seat Wen, how are you now compared to when you were at Huangbo? Nan said, "When he was at Huangbo, he used money as if it were mere dung;
now he is like a wealthy man of several generations, not spending a single coin in vain. From this on, he was respected by his contemporaries who had undergone thorough training.
After Master Nan entered nirvana, students gathered around him like clouds, and wherever he went, he established a monastic community.
In the fifth year of the Xīngníng era, Lín resided at Dàyú in Jūn Prefecture. Because the Master possessed spiritual practice, the assembly flocked to him in great numbers.
When the Prefect, Qian Gōngyí, came to visit and was surprised by the sudden increase in the number of meditators, he entered the Master’s quarters, yet found nothing extraordinary there.

The next day, he was commanded to take his meal. Just as the Master was about to take his seat at the table, a dog escaped from behind the screen curtains. The Master stepped aside slightly to avoid it.
Master Qian mocked him, saying, "A Chan practitioner is surely capable of subduing tigers; why, then, do you fear a dog?

The Master replied instantly, "It is easy to subdue a tiger lurking in a rocky ravine, but difficult to tame a dragon guarding its dwelling. Master Qian was greatly pleased and wished to hear the Way daily; he then vacated his own quarters for the Master.
The Emperor decreed that the Master should reside at Shou Temple. At that time, the Master was dining at the home of Chen, a local official of the district. When the imperial edict arrived, he fled.
Lord Qian had dozens of people from the same table arrested and, together with the monastic officials, sought him relentlessly, vowing not to stop until he was found.
Someone saw him at Xinfeng Mountain Temple; they rushed there immediately. Chen, seeing them, bowed his head and wept, saying, "The Master will not go."
"Our community is suffering. The Master said, "Because of me, you have been burdened in this way; therefore, I shall accept it" and subsequently propagated the Dharma.
Not long after, he moved his residence to the Puhua Chan Monastery on Mount Dong. Toward the end of the Yuanfeng era, he wished to travel to the mountains and waters of Eastern Wu;
he relinquished his dwelling and traveled eastward by small boat until he reached Mount Zhong, where he visited Chancellor Wang, the Prince of Shu. The Prince—

He had long known the Master’s name. Upon meeting him, he was filled with great joy. He invited the Master to stay overnight at Dinglin Hermitage. At that time, the Master [Wang] had recently recovered from an illness and delighted in hearing the teachings of the *śūnyatā* (emptiness) school.
Regretting his late acquaintance with the Master, he said to him: "In all the sutras, the time and place are invariably stated at the outset;

why is it that the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith Sutra* alone is not so? The Master replied: "That which is expounded in the Sudden Vehicle is intended to directly show sentient beings what is manifest in their daily lives."

It pertains to both the present and the past. Right now, this old monk and you, sir, have together entered the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-avabhāsa-garbha*) and sport within the *samādhi* of non-duality, acting as host and guest to one another;
this has nothing to do with time or place. Furthermore, it is said that the sutra states: "All sentient beings have fully realized perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)."
As for Guifeng’s change of "realization" (*zhèng*) to "endowment" (*jù*), claiming it was a scribal error—what is the meaning of this? The Master said:

"If the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* could be altered, then the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* could also be altered. Does not the *Vimalakīrti* say: 'Furthermore, one does not realize enlightenment by extinguishing sensation'?

Now, realizing enlightenment without extinguishing the aggregate of sensation is identical in meaning to the principle that all realize *Awakening of Mahāyāna*. This is because [the teachings of] the assembly..."
The arising and active manifestation of ignorance is precisely the Tathāgata’s fundamental great wisdom. Guifeng’s words were not correct.
Gong was greatly pleased and consequently donated his residence to establish a monastery to invite the Master as its founding patriarch.

Furthermore, he expanded the temple through the imperial gifts of medicine and provisions bestowed by Emperor Shenzong during his visits for inquiries after the Master's health; thus it was named Baoning. He also granted annual ordinations and purchased estates for the monastery.

He provided his lands for the benefit of students and personally composed a petition for ordination, which contained the phrase: "Possessing the power of the direct transmission alone, I forcefully refute frivolous arguments.
This describes the words of the Master. Furthermore, he requested [the Emperor] on behalf of the Master’s name, and the latter was granted purple robes and the title of Great Master Zhenjing.
In Jinling and Jianghuai, he held great assemblies for students who gathered like rice, hemp, millet, and reeds; the temple was newly renovated.

His quarters could not accommodate them; there was not a single day that scholar-officials did not pass through on their travels. Before the Master had even finished rinsing his mouth or washing his hands, the space outside his door was filled with visitors' shoes.
Finding himself nearly unable to endure such toil, he resolved to return to Gao'an. That very day he crossed the river, though the Chancellor tried to detain him, he would not comply.
He chose to settle for old age beneath the Nine Peaks and built a "Retirement for Old Age" hermitage (Tou-lao-an). [The year] Shao... [continued].
At the beginning of the Sage’s [reign], Imperial Censor Huang Gong Qingji was appointed as the Governor of Nankang. He vacated the seat at Guizong Temple to welcome the Master.

The Master said, "I am now so old and infirm; how could it be appropriate for me to again undergo the humiliation of being prostrated before to be welcomed or sent off? Please convey my thanks to Lord Huang."
He requested to die there. His disciples entreated him, saying, "The mountain is remote and provisions are scarce, yet the number of students increases daily.
Although your Master’s virtue and seniority are great, your spirit remains robust. Since the time of the two Great Sages, Zong and You, the monastic communities have been like extinguished embers.
We pray that you will not forget your ancestors and will fulfill the hopes of the people. Having no other choice, he then departed. Previously, Huang...
The Duke once caught sight of the Master in the midst of a large assembly at the Chancellor’s residence.

After the Master had departed, the Chancellor said to the Duke, "I have observed many monks, yet none have been like this old man. Consequently, the Duke treated him with full courtesy and exerted himself to bring him there.

At the various monasteries of Mount Lu, the practitioners had long prided themselves on luxury; those who resided there were accustomed to comfort and warmth, but the Master invariably lived in austerity, causing the students to find it difficult.

They were intoxicated by mere words and deluded by superficiality. Although the Master, employing his unimpeded eloquence, rebuked their biased views, it was not until less than a year had passed that these views became widespread as a prevailing trend.

Three years later, in the tenth month of the first year of the Chongning era (1102), when Chancellor Zhang Gong Shangying was dispatched to govern Hongfu, he passed through Guizong on his way and visited the Master at Jingming Hermitage.
The following year, he invited the Master to reside at Shimen. It was the tenth month of the first year of the Chongning era.

Manifesting illness, on the night of the sixteenth day, he bathed, changed his robes, and sat in the full lotus posture. When the assembly requested him to preach the Dharma, the Master smiled and said:
"This year I am seventy-eight; the four elements are parting from one another. Since fire and wind have already dispersed, there is no need for further words as I depart."
He left instructions to his disciples, all concerning the great matters of the School of the Gate (the Chan school), and did not speak of private affairs.

When he finished speaking, he passed away at the age of seventy-eight, having been in the monastic order for fifty-two years. On the day of his cremation, flames of five colors arose, and white light ascended into the sky.
Wherever the smoke reached, *śarīra* relics were distributed; more than a thousand monastics and laypeople obtained them, and those remaining were beyond counting.
The stupa was erected at the foot of Duxiu Peak. The Master’s pure sincerity and compassionate love were innate; his temperament was lofty and transcendent, singular and extraordinary.
Whether encountering those near or distant, noble or humble, he would always offer a warm countenance and gentle words, treating them all with equal reverence.

In presiding over the monastic community, his legal standards were extremely strict; those who violated the regulations were invariably punished without pardon. For this reason, he sat upon the seat of enlightenment five times.
He was a model for all quarters, having attained the Samādhi of Līlā (Playful Mastery) and possessing the eloquence of joyful exposition.

With the sharp edge of his words and the blade of his wisdom, he felled the forest of heterodoxy like falling clouds or crashing boulders. He revealed right view with such brilliance that it was as clear as the sun in a blue sky;

yet, though everyone considered themselves to have reached the profound depths, when it came to entering the inner chamber and meeting the pivot of the teaching, they were like [climbing] a copper cliff or an iron wall.
He could not be grasped or relied upon. By nature he delighted in giving; he bestowed whatever he had. Aside from his staff and alms bowl, he did not keep a single coin.

For over fifty years he traveled and preached the Dharma, wearing simple clothes and tattered robes while maintaining a carefree and self-reliant composure. He possessed a great affinity with the people of Jiangxi;
the populace believed in his transformation, painting his portrait in every household and offering him worship whenever they ate or drank. His dharma-heir disciples... [text continues]
Huangbo Daoquan, Doushuai Congyue, and the others—ten or more in total—represent the general outline of his life.
As for the subtle and profound essence of his Way, it cannot be fully described by brush or ink. I have ventured to discuss it:
his casting aside the scholar’s cap to enter the Way was like that of Danxia; his pursuit of the study of sutras and treatises followed by sudden awakening was like that of Nanquan. Seeking...
The Master’s hardships were formidable and never diminished, much like Xuefeng; his teaching was unrestrained and versatile, harmonizing both doctrine and practice, much like Dazhu;
and his brilliance and magnificence in upholding the tradition were like those of Baizhang. This is not my own word.

These are the words of a scholar from the monastic forests. Alas! To possess fully all the excellences of the ancient masters, one may truly be called a great synthesizer who brings glory to the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Chongning era.
A Disciple, [Name], respectfully prostrates himself.
An Offering Text for Master Yungan:
When I was nine years old, I first knew there was a teacher. Whether awake or asleep, I delighted in him and yearned to behold his countenance. It was in Xinfeng that I came to recognize my teacher.
With a compassion equal to that for one's own parents, he joyfully stroked my head and directed me to take up the *kundikā* (water jar) to travel far to the great city of Liang.

There I shaved my hair and returned to visit Jiufeng. His majestic virtue was so awe-inspiring that all things flourished and grew, like plants nourished by frost, snow, rain, and dew. It was the Master who brought me to fulfillment.
Sublime as the four seasons, beneath the Purple Heavens and along the banks of the Led River, for seven years past and present, the dragon has arisen and the clouds have followed.
Whether through envy and slander or through love and care, he has never abandoned me. When I formerly left the mountains...

The Master then offered these words: "You are young yet already displaying brilliance; you will surely achieve great things in the end. I am old now, and I fear I shall not have the opportunity to see you again.

I point to these two sons of mine and entrust them to your instruction. You may reprimand or scold them as you see fit, but they must never be separated from one another. Your virtuous words remain in my ears."

Eight years have passed since the seasons changed. You, Master, have been enshrined in a new stupa, and I too have presented my offerings. In the past, when you had already passed away, I sat before your remains and wept.

All of you left behind the essence of your enlightenment; from afar, you requested an inscription for me. Once my task was completed and I returned, I collapsed upon the ground. Mountains and rivers lie between us in阻隔 (separation).

For a long time we have been severed from correspondence; now I alone have brought Xizu to travel a thousand li to bid you farewell, thereby fulfilling my long-held aspiration. Even in death, I shall have no regrets or sorrow.
Throughout your life, your accumulated virtues were towering and magnificent; that your legacy will surely flourish in the future is beyond any doubt. How could I not be inspired by this?
Superiors repay their private kindness;

the cicada repairs the pagoda of the Cloud Hermitage, departing at dawn but returning at dusk, never forgetting its origin. The crow’s feathers grow and it returns to feed its parents, for it knows the debt of gratitude.
What can be observed in those who merely possess teeth and wear hair? They are not even equal to the crows that feed their young or the frogs in the fields.

Only the eaves of Yun’an Monastery remain, where famous mountains are spread out like a chessboard; yet the egg-shaped stupas have already crumbled, decaying amidst the vast wilderness, and the chambers contain only rotting pillars.
The granaries hold old red rice; hearing this, one does not complete [the task]. Idle chatter has already ensued; wishing to proceed, one stops midway.
Truly, this is no human being. — *Cloud Hermitage True Praise* (Yun'an zhen zan)
Yun’an emerged from the lineage of Huanglong; he was the ninth-generation descendant of Linji. His spiritual nature was exceptionally sublime and his realization vast and profound.
In pointing out the essentials of the mind, his eloquence was like that of Caoqi; in discerning the vehicles of the teachings, his discourse was like that of Zao Bo;
in composing verses, his phrasing was like that of Master Zhigong; and in his practical realization, his precision was like that of Yongjia. By the time he retired to live at Yun’an, he had already—
At over seventy years of age, his illusions were entirely extinguished and his wisdom-light was perfectly round; one can thus imagine the lingering influence of his remaining legacy.
His disciple Dehong respectfully prostrates himself with his head to the ground and offers this eulogy:
Thus abiding in the realm, where the seer and the conditions for seeing are like the subject and object in a dream;
possessing only the true eye amidst the center and periphery of honey, one enters this samādhi like a wondrous lotus.
The living intent of the Patriarchs, the secret mechanism of the Tathāgata, brings sentient beings to fulfillment like the soaring of the *kūṇapeng* bird.
He brought about self-transformation, Not relying on awakening through others. Standing out preeminent within the forest of monks, He shed light upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
He passed away in Shanxi, And was born in Jiangnan. Five colors shone in the darkness; "Yun'an," inscribed by the world for the hand-letter of Yun'an.
(Three Poems Inscribed for the Hand-letter of Yun'an)
Master Nanshan was skilled at copying the calligraphy of Lord Lu. At that time, among those who followed Master Nan, there were none who did not study his style;

yet, none emerged to surpass Yun’an. The Elder Zhaomo once viewed this work with Dehong and admired it incessantly, remarking that it was no less than that of the Imperial Preceptor Yang—a true man of the Way. He held it in high esteem. (Chongning 5)
On the eighteenth day of the tenth month of this year, a disciple [name] inscribed this.
A letter from Venerable Yúnān to a donor: I have humbly read it as if receiving words of instruction. The monastic community is desolate and cold.
There is no longer the same as in former days; this old man knows he shall not see him again, much less his calligraphy or speech.
His disciple [Name], weeping, respectfully records this. The above is a verse sent by Yun’an to Zhang Huizhuan. I have not seen Huizhuan for twenty years; I hear that...
His diligence has improved daily; he is truly one who can follow and receive the words of Yun’an.
When the Venerable Cheng came from Xuānfàn to inquire after his teacher and whether Huìyuǎn was well, I happened to recall a previous verse.

I then wrote it down and gave it to Cheng, instructing him to return and present it to Huìyuǎn so that they might compare it with the original version of that day for any discrepancies. Written by me.
In praise of Yun’an of Bashan Valley:

When Yun’an was residing at Mount Lu, Huang Tingjian (Shanggu) visited him. Together they strolled by Luan Creek and sat upon a large rock, where they carved their names into the stone in bold characters.
Their shared delight in the Dharma was like that of Huangbo and Lord Pei; thus, this eulogy was composed. Twenty years later...
In another year, [the manuscript] was obtained at the home of the Mao family in Hengyang. It was brought back to Changsha Kaifa by the Elder Jueci, who was indeed its direct descendant.
At that time, he was twenty-three years old; he immediately entrusted it to Linji’s orthodox lineage so that it might circulate without interruption.
Thus, he had no cause for shame. This praise is offered with deep reverence. The Mid-Autumn Festival of the fifth year of the Xuanhua era.
The Day Before: Inscription.
Cloud Hermitage’s Birthday:
Reaching into the void of the kalpa of emptiness, one divides it into fragments as small as a speck of dust. All is transparently without gap or vacancy; standing alone, it is never stale or worn.
I ask you: how does seeing before sound compare to intimacy after the crown? The waves of birth and death obscure it, yet this very moment it leaks forth.
On the fourth day of the seventh month, I dreamed during the day that Master Yun’an instructed me; after a long time, I awoke and wrote this to show Chao’ran.
Who calls me from my midday nap at the summer window? In the quiet courtyard, I hear only the water circling the steps. The lingering words from my dreams can still be recalled;
the images left upon the walls remain as they were. The cushioned pearls surely reveal the clenched fists; the sitting mat must have worn through where the knees rested.
The pagoda atop the layered peaks strains my failing eyesight—when shall we sweep these crumbling bricks together with you?
The pagoda at Yun’an has a pair of paulownia trees. I compose this verse to send to my nephew, who has not returned for ten years;

the ancestral teacher’s pagoda there is said to have twin paulownias guarding the stone roots. A Prabhūtaratna Buddha would surely share half his seat, and the forest deity would manifest his own form before him.
Having finished this poem while sitting facing the Southern Mountain Patriarch, I transcribe it and send it to the Jade One in the mountains.
Jianyin said, "In the future, when you build a hut in the shade, I shall offer incense and prayers at the seasonal festivals to become your neighbor."
